content:
The word monk comes from the Old English munuc, based on the Greek monakhos ‘solitary,’ from monos ‘alone.’ It is mostly used for men, while monastic women are called nuns. Some religions and regions don't allow women to become ordained. A monk is a person who practices religious asceticism (intense self-discipline) through monastic living. They either live alone or with other monks. They abandon society and worldly pleasures and live to serve others and god. Many religions have monks, including Buddhism, Hinduism, Christianity, Jainism, and Sikhism. Monks may not ask for anything, including food unless they are ill. However, they are allowed to accept gifts. They can eat and cover modest living expenses with what the public gives them. Lifestyle customs, requirements, and rituals vary by region and religion. One group called the Marathon Monks, uses extreme endurance through running to pursue enlightenment.

The monks of Mount Hiei, Japan, undertake a challenge known as the ‘kaihōgyō.’ The purpose of the spiritual challenge is to achieve enlightenment through endurance, deprivation, and discipline. They must complete 1,000 days of long-distance running over the course of seven years. The monks wear white, the Buddhist color of death, while they attempt to complete the challenge. The white attire reminds them that the task before them will take them to the limits of their ability and life itself. The point of the challenge is to bring the practitioner as close to death as possible. It is designed to elicit massive appreciation for life. The constant mental and physical exhaustion leaves the practitioner empty and open to spiritual knowledge. Many religions have their own set of rituals and rites of passage. Some rituals mark a transition to a new stage of life. Others break the ego and rid the self of worldly attachments.

In addition to the white attire the Mount Hiei monks don during the “kaihōgyō” running challenge, they wear other specific garments. A long, canoe-shaped hat with rolled-up sides sits atop their heads, and they tuck a “rokumon-sen” coin into it so they can pay to cross the mythological Sanzu River to the land of the dead in case they die during the challenge. The monks are not allowed to remove their white robes or hats during their runs. Although they navigate treacherous terrain with jagged rocks and snakes, the monks wear handmade straw and linen sandals. The running monks have been wearing straw and linen sandals for one thousand years. A switch to more modern running shoes would be an act of indulgence. Traditional footwear isn't very sturdy; a runner may go through several pairs daily. Amazingly, bystander reports attest to the health of the runner's feet throughout their journey.

As the Marathon Monks carry out the “kaihōgyō” running challenge, they must follow a prescribed route. Deviation from the route is forbidden and there are specific stops and tasks along the way. The monks have to visit several shrines and recite specific chants and prayers. A steady pace is necessary to reach daily checkpoints. The monks are not allowed to take personal breaks. Additionally, smoking and drinking alcohol are prohibited. The rules are in place to prepare the body for the challenge and ensure maximum dedication and clarity of purpose. The selection process for the “kaihōgyō” happens after the first 100 days of practice. The “gyōja” (practice person) asks senior monks to complete the remaining 900 days. Withdrawal from the challenge is possible in the first 100 days, but from day 101 onwards, the monk is no longer allowed to withdraw. Historically, a monk must either complete the course or take their own life.
